title: Name the Risk
blurb: The OWASP Top 10 (2025 edition) is the industry's list of the most critical web app risks. Match each category to what it actually means — the vocabulary you're expected to know.

levels.title: L1 · The ones you'll meet most
levels.prompt: Match each OWASP 2025 category to its meaning.

right.label: Users act outside their permissions — reading or changing data that isn't theirs (e.g. changing an id in the URL).
Untrusted input is interpreted as code or a command — SQL injection, OS commands, and XSS all live here.
Sensitive data isn't protected — weak or missing hashing/encryption, secrets in code, no HTTPS.
Weaknesses in proving who a user is — weak passwords, no MFA, broken sessions, credential stuffing.
Insecure defaults or missing hardening — unnecessary features on, dev error pages in prod, no security headers.

levels.explain: Broken Access Control = doing what you shouldn't; Injection = input treated as code; Cryptographic Failures = unprotected data; Authentication Failures = weak identity proof; Security Misconfiguration = insecure setup.

failStates.title: Authentication vs. Access Control
failStates.explain: Authentication (A07) is proving WHO you are. Access Control (A01) is what you're allowed to DO once you're in. A logged-in user reading someone else's data is broken access control, not an auth failure.

failStates.title: Crypto isn't injection
failStates.explain: Cryptographic Failures is about unprotected sensitive data. Injection is untrusted input being executed. Different roots, different fixes.

levels.title: L2 · The rest of the ten
levels.prompt: Match the remaining OWASP 2025 categories to their meaning.

right.label: Risk from what you depend on — vulnerable/outdated packages, compromised build or CI/CD pipelines.
Flaws baked into the design itself — missing threat modeling, business-logic gaps clean code can't fix.
Trusting code or data that could be tampered with — unsafe deserialization, unsigned updates.
Attacks go unnoticed — no logs for security events, no monitoring or alerting on suspicious activity.
Errors handled insecurely — leaking stack traces, failing open, or swallowing exceptions so checks are skipped.

levels.explain: Supply Chain = your dependencies; Insecure Design = the plan is flawed; Integrity Failures = trusting tampered code/data; Logging & Alerting = you never see the attack; Mishandling Exceptions = errors handled unsafely (new in 2025).

failStates.title: Design flaw vs. error handling
failStates.explain: Insecure Design (A06) is a missing or flawed control at the design level. Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (A10) is specifically about how the code reacts when something throws or goes wrong.

failStates.title: Integrity vs. supply chain
failStates.explain: Supply Chain (A03) is about the components you pull in. Integrity Failures (A08) is about trusting data/code that could be modified — like deserializing attacker-controlled input.
